title: Foundation Visual Encoders Are Secretly Few-Shot Anomaly Detectors
one_liner: Foundation models already know what normal images look like; just teach them to project defective images back onto normal and measure the gap.
lead: Industrial inspection needs to spot defects in products with only a handful of examples. The paper finds that large pre-trained vision models (trained on millions of natural images) already have learned what normal looks like. By training a simple, lightweight neural network operator to map anomalies back toward normality, you can detect defects without needing to see many examples of the bad thing.

paras: In a factory, a camera watches for defects. Most products are fine. A few are broken or scratched. The trouble: you have maybe 2 or 3 photos of defects, but thousands of normal products. With so few bad examples, how do you train a detector?

A naive approach would be: collect lots of images of both good and bad, then train a detector from scratch. But with only 2 examples of defects, you have nothing to train on. The detector will just memorize those 2 pictures and fail on any slightly different defect. It is drowning in randomness.

callout.html: You cannot detect what is broken if you have almost never seen it broken.

panels.title: 1. Massive pre-training
panels.caption: A foundation encoder trained on millions of photos learns what normal looks like.

panels.title: 2. Normal and defective embeddings diverge
panels.caption: When you pass a normal image through, you get one list of numbers. A defective image gives a very different list.

panels.title: 3. The projector learns the pull
panels.viz_args: Teach a light net to gently nudge defective numbers toward normal ones.
panels.caption: A tiny trained operator pulls defective number-lists back toward the normal region.

panels.title: 4. Measure the tug
panels.caption: How far did we have to pull? That distance is the anomaly score.

panels.title: 5. Defects stand out
panels.caption: Normal images need almost no pull. Defects need a big tug. High score means broken.

steps.text: Use a pre-trained model (DINOv3 or CLIP) that was trained on millions of normal images. Do not change it.
Take your 2-3 normal images and artificially introduce scratches, cuts, or patches (copy-paste synthetic damage). Now you have a handful of genuine and fake-defective samples.
Pass fake-defective images through the encoder and get their number-lists. Train a small neural net to map those lists closer to what normal lists look like.
For any image, compute how far its embeddings are from normal after projection. Big distance means anomaly. Small distance means normal.
On a real factory image, compute the gap. If high, raise the alarm. No re-training needed.

object.h2: The single object the paper changes
paras: The paper trains one small lightweight operator (a nonlinear projector) that sits on top of the frozen number-lists from the encoder. Nothing else moves. The projector is the only learnable part.

hidden.h2: Embedding distance: how far off normal
hidden.name: Anomaly distance
paras: The hidden quantity is the distance between a projected embedding and what a normal embedding should look like. Think of it as a gap: the encoder produces a list of numbers for any image; you measure how far those numbers sit from where normal images cluster.
The paper uses the projector to shrink the gap for synthetic anomalies during training, then at test time, it measures whether the gap stays small or grew large. Large gap means defect.

heat.caption: Darker means bigger gap from normal. The projector learns to shrink synthetic defects; at test time, any large gap signals anomaly.

reads.html: An embedding (just a list of numbers the model creates for any image) measures anomaly distance by how far the defective number-list sits from the normal number-list. Big difference means broken. Small difference means fine.

The paper learns a projection operator that maps anomaly-aware number-lists closer to reference number-lists. During training, the loss shrinks the distance between the projected defective list and the normal reference list using a standard distance metric.

paras: Pre-trained vision models have already learned a shape in number-space where all normal images cluster tightly together (like a valley). Defective images fall outside this normal cluster. Imagine a valley-shaped surface in a high-dimensional space where all normal images nest together. Defective images sit off the valley floor.

If you know where normal sits (which the pre-trained encoder does), you can measure how far any image is from that normal zone. You pull a rope from the defective image down toward the normal cluster and measure the tension. That pulling distance is your anomaly score. The projector learns exactly where the normal cluster sits so it can perform this measuring task.

Why does this work with only 2 examples? Because the encoder already knows normal—it was trained on millions of images. You only need a tiny dataset to teach the projector where the specific normal cluster lives for your product. The projector itself is so small that a handful of synthetic anomalies suffice to train it, so it naturally generalizes to real defects it has never seen.

stages.s: Frozen encoder maps images to embeddings
Projector pulls defective embeddings toward normal
Measure the distance before and after projection
Anomaly score: how far was the pull?

math.words: Minimize the distance between the projected defective embedding and the normal reference embedding.
symbols: the projector (a small neural network we train)
the embedding of a synthesized defective image
the embedding of the corresponding normal image
distance measurement (usually Euclidean norm, the straight-line distance between two number-lists)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Imagine embeddings are just 2 numbers (instead of 768). Normal image: f_r = [3, 4]. Defective image before projection: f_s = [8, 15].
Projector is trained to shrink this. After training, φ(f_s) = [3.5, 4.5] (close to normal).
At test time, measure how much the defect was pulled. Large gap (12.1) in the raw embedding means anomaly. Small gap (0.71 after projection) in a normal test image confirms it is normal.

math.note: The projector learns a custom nudge that pulls anomalies toward the normal valley; distance shrinkage reveals whether something is defective.

charts.title: Old approach (train from scratch)
charts.note: Training a detector from scratch on 2 examples overfits and memorizes. Needs many samples and large models.

charts.title: FoundAD (projection onto pre-learned normal)
charts.note: Using a frozen encoder and tiny projector generalizes from 2 examples to real defects. Tiny model, fast answers at test time, broad generalization.

items.html: If the pre-trained encoder was trained on data very different from your factory images (e.g. trained on art, you inspect metal), the normal cluster it learned is misaligned. The projector cannot fix this. Use an encoder trained on natural images or industrial photos.

items.b: Synthetic defects do not match real defects.
items.html: If your artificial scratches look nothing like real factory defects, the projector learns a wrong rule and fails on genuine damage. Synthetic anomaly generation must match real failure modes.

items.b: Multiple defect types in one product.
items.html: A single defect model assumes anomalies form one cluster. If your factory has scratches, dents, and discoloration as separate failure modes, a single projector may confuse them. The paper handles multi-class detection, but each class needs its own normal reference.

Use a foundation encoder trained on diverse natural images. Generate synthetic anomalies that resemble real failures. If you have multiple defect types, train separate projectors or gather a few examples of each. Test on held-out real defects.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple anomaly detector on one industrial dataset. Use a pre-trained DINOv3 or CLIP encoder (frozen, no changes). Gather 2-3 normal product images and 5-10 real defective images for testing.

Artificially synthesize 10-20 fake anomalies from your normal images by pasting patches or introducing scratches. Train a small projector (2-3 layer neural net) to map synthetic defects back to the normal embedding space. Then test on your real defects.

Compute an anomaly score for each test image: how far was the embedding before and after projection? Plot the scores: normal products should have low scores, real defects should have high scores. The gap between them proves the projector found the right normal valley.
demo.metric_eq: AUROC = area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve; plot normal-image scores vs defect-image scores and measure overlap.
demo.closing: A clear gap between normal and defect scores proves the method works: the frozen encoder already knew normal, and the projector just learned to measure how far from normal any image sits.
